prompts.title: The Vanishing Archive
prompts.body: A log service parses a 256 MiB input buffer. Downstream work retains only a 24-byte identifier from each selected record for several minutes. The input must then be reused for the next batch. Your benchmark rewards low allocation counts, but the incident report complains about peak live memory. Choose a representation before you inspect the consequences. Assume the selected identifiers are a small fraction of the original buffer and do not need to preserve the original allocation identity.

options.text: Keep slices into the reusable buffer
Retain an Arc to the whole batch
Copy the selected identifiers at the queue boundary

feedbackByOption.1: The borrowing relationship prevents reuse while the slices remain usable. That compiler error identifies the incompatible storage policy. Extending annotations does not make the buffer independent. This choice works if consumers finish before reuse or if you change the owner and stop reusing this allocation; it does not meet the requirements as stated.
feedbackByOption.2: Shared ownership keeps the original bytes alive for views or validated ranges. It also prevents overwriting those bytes while readers still need them, and one tiny identifier retains the entire 256 MiB. This design fits a different contract that allows a separate receive buffer and makes dense retention worth its memory cost.
feedbackByOption.3: The queue owns compact strings independent of the batch. This deliberately spends allocations and byte copies to release the much larger source and permit reuse. Measure selected-byte volume and allocator costs, but compare them against peak retained memory rather than declaring zero-copy the winner by definition.

prompts.title: Remix the scenario
prompts.body: Downstream analysis now retains nearly every byte. The producer may rotate to another receive buffer while readers retain the old one. Re-evaluate the three actions and explain how retention density and the number of live batches affect your choice.

prompts.title: The Ghost Payment
prompts.body: A request future times out after sending a payment command. The connection then disappears. Your local request value is dropped cleanly. The remote service may have processed the command, but no acknowledgement reached you. The business requires that one purchase must not be charged twice. Choose your next action. The service has a status lookup and an idempotency-key mechanism, but their retention and deduplication contracts must be checked.

options.text: Retry immediately with a fresh operation identifier
Reuse the key and treat deduplication as automatic
Record an uncertain outcome and reconcile under the peer contract

feedbackByOption.1: A new identifier can make the retry look like a second purchase. Dropping the future did not reverse the remote effect. This action is suitable only if duplicate execution is acceptable or another layer prevents it; the stated purchase invariant does not permit that assumption.
feedbackByOption.2: A stable key is useful only under the peer's documented scope, retention period, payload matching, and failure behavior. If the record expires before retry or different payloads share a key, your local type cannot repair the protocol. First establish the remote contract rather than treating the presence of a key field as a guarantee.
feedbackByOption.3: Keep the original operation identity and the exact request meaning. Consult the peer's status and idempotency behavior, then retry or reconcile according to that contract. An inconclusive lookup may leave the outcome uncertain. This is an explicit protocol state, not a reason to manufacture a success or failure locally.

prompts.title: The Hollow Lock
prompts.body: A shared cache calls a slow user-supplied loader while holding its global mutex. The loader can recursively request another key, and two requests for the same key can trigger an expensive external operation. Product wants low contention and one active loader per key. Choose an initial redesign. A valid answer must account for reentrancy, failure, and abandoned loads rather than merely moving a lock statement.

options.text: Keep the global lock and forbid nothing else
Release the lock and allow every miss to load
Install a per-key loading state and coordinate waiters

feedbackByOption.1: The recursive call can attempt to acquire the mutex already held by the loader. A global lock also serializes unrelated keys. This does not satisfy the stated reentrancy and contention requirements. A non-reentrant contract could be a different design, but it must be explicit and still needs an argument for lock duration.
feedbackByOption.2: This removes the global lock from user code and can be a sound, useful cache policy. It also allows duplicate loads for the same key, so it fails the one-active-loader requirement as stated. If duplicate pure work is acceptable, this simpler policy may be the right tradeoff; external effects need additional care.
feedbackByOption.3: Publish ready or failed and wake waiters even if a load panics or is abandoned. Run loaders outside the global lock and impose a fixed key order: a loader may request only higher-ranked keys. Reject other nested requests before starting or waiting on a load. This prevents self-waits and cross-key cycles such as A waiting for B while B waits for A.

prompts.title: Remix the scenario
prompts.body: Let callers cancel while waiting and permit the initiating loader to disappear. Explain how waiters get a terminal outcome and when they can retry. Test two simultaneous loaders that request each other's keys and identify which request must fail.

Test A and B loading together and reject the backwards request before it can block.

prompts.title: Training encounter 3
prompts.body: Choose a function from your own codebase and write three claims: one enforced by types, one requiring runtime validation, and one requiring a protocol with another component. Name a verification method for each.
prompts.feedback: An example type claim is that a returned view cannot outlive its source, checked through compilation. A runtime claim is that an index is within the initialized prefix, checked through validation and boundary tests. A protocol claim is that retries do not duplicate a remote effect, checked through operation identifiers, peer behavior, and fault-injection tests. No single tool establishes all three.

notes: 1. Generalize transfer to a balance type whose arithmetic can return errors and whose assignment may run a destructor. Identify which parts of the original failure argument no longer follow automatically.
Mission lens. Build and defend one coherent in-memory system whose ownership, state, progress, and verification claims agree.

title: The Last Unstated Assumption

prompts.title: The Last Unstated Assumption
prompts.body: Build a finite repair simulator using the book’s ideas: immutable parsed configuration, a versioned local store, bounded work admission, and a fake remote peer that can lose replies. Choose a modest scenario such as updating station settings. Implement enough of the path to run a successful request, a stale transaction, and a lost acknowledgment. Supply an ownership diagram, a wait graph, and three precise invariants. For each invariant, name the implementation mechanism and evidence that supports it. Introduce one controlled failure after acceptance and show the reported outcome without silently losing the request or claiming the remote effect never occurred. Unsafe code is optional; if used, include its proof obligations and explain why the safe representation was insufficient.
criteria: Keep the scope finite and runnable without a real network or deployed database.
Do not claim durability, exactly-once delivery, or proof of soundness from the simulator.
Any memory bound must name queues, payload retention, snapshots, and admitted work.
prompts.feedback: Your draft is saved. Compare it with the encounter constraints, then reveal a hint or the debrief when you are ready.

notes: State the invariant and how you would falsify it before implementing a repair. The hints reveal progressively more of the argument.

title: Restore Ferrum

prompts.title: Side quest
prompts.body: Invite another developer to choose one hostile change: a retained old snapshot, a forgotten guard, a collector failure, a malformed frame, or a reused operation ID. Predict which invariant it challenges before running anything. Repair the design or narrow the promise, then update the evidence. Your final achievement is the ability to explain the repair, not merely to recover a passing test.
prompts.feedback: Your side quest evidence is saved. Mark the side quest in your log once you can explain the added constraint and its effect.

notes: Optional twist. Keeper of Explicit Invariants
